title: Simul vs GM Rabiega · you Black · Alapin Sicilian
event: Jubiläumssimultan 75 Jahre SC Weisse Dame · GM Robert Rabiega (DWZ 2421) · no clock, move when he arrives
logNote: Simul 19.09.26 vs GM Rabiega, ½ — offered by the GM in a lost position (about +5 at move 45). Saw 26.Re8+ Kf7 and stopped there; 27.Rc8! wins c6. Then 28…Ra6 handed over the seventh (29.Rb7! was winning). Lost from 31…c5 on.

steps.name: 1 One move more
steps.title: After 25.Re1, Black to move
steps.prompt: You played 25…Ra7. Name the reply you looked at, then write every move after it — until a pawn falls.

mixups.key: That is the game. 27.Rb8 lets you back in with 27…Ke6, and you were still only slightly worse. The move you had to calculate is 27.Rc8 — it attacks c6, and a7 cannot defend it.

steps.key:
Ply 3 is 27.Rc8. The rook steps in front of your weak pawn, not behind it: 27…Bc4 28.Rxc6 and c6 is gone with the rook on a7 watching. You saw 26.Re8+, you saw 26…Kf7, and you stopped there because Kf7 looked fine. It is fine. The move after it is not.

25…Rc8 keeps the balance: the rook defends c6 along the rank and the file is not White's anymore.

steps.name: 2 Diagnose
steps.title: After 25.Re1, Black to move
steps.prompt: One open file, one weak pawn. Decide where the rook belongs before you calculate.

questions.name: weak
questions.label: 2.1 Which black pawn is the target?
questions.hint: It appeared on move 24 and cannot be defended by another pawn.

questions.name: entry
questions.label: 2.2 White's rook entry squares on the open file
questions.hint: Two of them. One is only a check; the other hits the pawn.

questions.name: job
questions.label: 2.3 What does the rook on a7 defend that is actually attacked?

steps.key:
The target is c6, made on 24…bxc6. No pawn can ever defend it — only a piece can, and only from the c-file or the sixth rank.

Entry squares: e8 and c8. e8 is a check and nothing more. c8 is the move: it attacks c6 and takes the file for good.

The rook on a7 defends nothing that is attacked. It guards the seventh rank and the b7 square, and neither is under fire. Your own sentence from game 1, now against you: "Red1 is pseudo-activity; Black can put a rook on the file." Here you were the one who left the file alone.

steps.name: 3 Calculate
steps.title: Four rook moves from move 25. Play each one to the end.
steps.prompt: Two branches show only the first moves — write the rest before you touch the board (Enter checks it). The other two you play through. The step's key opens once all four are locked.

questions.name: whyc8
questions.label: After 25…Rc8, White plays 26.Re3 Bc4 27.b3. Why is the c6 pawn not falling here?

questions.name: re8
questions.label: 25…Re8 offers a trade. In one word, why is it not a trade?

branches.label: Ra7 Re8+ Kf7 Rc8 Bc4 Rxc6
branches.key: The line you stopped two moves short of. A pawn down, both your remaining pawn islands loose, and the rook on a7 has nothing to do. This is a clear White advantage, not a nuance.

branches.label: Ra7 Re8+ Kf7 Rb8 Ke6 Bb4 (game)
branches.key: The game. 27.Rb8 goes after b6 instead of c6 and you got the king to e6 in time. You were let off — the punishment was 27.Rc8. Do not file this position as "Ra7 was playable".

branches.label: Rc8 Re3 Bc4 b3 Ba6
branches.key: Dead level. The rook on c8 defends c6 sideways, so the bishop is free to go hunting on the a6–f1 diagonal. Nothing can enter. This is what the position was worth before you moved.

branches.label: Re8 Rxe8+ Kf7 Re7+
branches.key: Not a trade — a check. Your king is on g8 and cannot reach e8, so the rook is simply gone. The same one-ply habit in its crudest form: you look at the capture you like and not at the plus sign behind it.

steps.key: All four. Rc8 holds, Ra7 loses a pawn by force, Re8 loses a rook. The difference between the first two is not judgement — it is three more ply.

steps.name: 4 The seventh
steps.title: After 28.Bb4, Black to move
steps.prompt: Three moves later, the same rook. This time it was doing a job. Find what leaving costs.

questions.name: guard
questions.label: 4.1 What is the rook on a7 guarding now that it was not guarding on move 25?

questions.name: missed
questions.label: 4.2 After 28…Ra6, which move did White miss?

branches.label: Ra6 Rb7 g5 Re7+ Kf5 Rxh7 (game move, punished)
branches.key: 29.Rb7! and the seventh rank is his. h7 falls, then g7, and the a6 rook is defending a pawn that nobody is attacking. Winning for White. In the game he played 29.Re8+ instead and you were back to one pawn down.

branches.label: b5 Re8+ Kf7 Rc8 g5
branches.key: Push the attacked pawn, keep the rook. b6 was the reason you wanted Ra6 — so move b6 and the reason disappears. The rook stays on the seventh, h7 and g7 stay defended, and you are a pawn worse instead of lost.

steps.key: Move 25: the rook on a7 defended nothing and you put it there. Move 28: the rook on a7 defended g7 and h7 and you took it away. Both times you decided where the rook belongs without playing the opponent's entry move — 27.Rc8, 29.Rb7. Name his entry square first, then choose.

steps.name: 5 Log
steps.title: A draw you were given, honestly tagged
steps.prompt: The result says ½. The board at the end says lost. Tag the game, not the result.

questions.name: why
questions.label: 5.1 What cost the half point first?

options.label: 31…c5: opened it up when a pawn down
25…Ra7 and 28…Ra6 — the same rook, the same missing move

questions.name: lost
questions.label: 5.2 The result says ½. From which move was the position lost?
questions.hint: The evaluation crosses two pawns once and never comes back.

steps.key:
The half point was offered, not earned. At move 45 White is more than five pawns up and the a-pawn is running. Late in a four-and-a-half-hour simul a GM offers draws to finish the evening. Rabiega's 17:2 (+15 =4 -0) is his statistic; do not file this as a defence.

Lost from 31…c5. Before it you were a pawn worse and suffering; after 32.dxc5 bxc5 33.Rxc5 you were two pawns down with nothing for them. Before that, 28…Ra6 had already given up the seventh, and 25…Ra7 had started it.

Tag calculation. The opening was fine and the middlegame was level right up to move 25 — the whole game turned on two rook moves, and both times the move you did not make was the opponent's entry move.

Game 1: you stopped at the reply you disliked (…a6). Game 2: you stopped at the recapture you liked (Bxf5). Here: you stopped at the move that looked fine (…Kf7). Three games, one habit. The move after the one that looks fine is the move.

No clock, but he arrives and you must move. That is the argument for the habit, not against it: when there is no time to calculate deep, the one question that still fits is where does his rook come in? — c8 on move 25, b7 on move 28. Ask it first and both moves choose themselves.
